name: Fake tooth caps / press-on veneers

lead: Press-on veneers and fake tooth caps are removable shells that sit over the front teeth to change their apparent shape or shade. The change is visible as soon as they are placed, for a more even, brighter smile.

They are non-prescription products and differ from dentist-made veneers, which are thin layers of composite or porcelain bonded to the tooth. The shell sits over the natural teeth, usually without bonding or tooth preparation. No published studies on the retail products were found.

paras: People buy them over the counter, fit them over their teeth at home and wear them for photos, events or short periods, then take them out. They are used as a temporary try-out of a look.
Safety and fit have not been studied in published research, and professional veneer literature does not cover these products.

lead: Press-on veneers and fake tooth caps are non-prescription cosmetic covers that are placed over the front of the teeth to change their apparent shape or shade, and are usually removable. They differ from dental veneers, which are thin layers of composite or porcelain bonded to the tooth by a dentist [1].
Published research specifically on over-the-counter press-on products was not found. Background on professional veneers comes from general references.

paras: Dental veneers were invented by California dentist Charles Pincus in 1928 as a temporary way to alter actors' teeth on film sets, and in 1937 he made acrylic versions held by denture adhesive [1]. Permanent porcelain veneers became possible after 1982 work on etching and bonding porcelain [1].

Wikipedia reports that preparing teeth for veneers can remove a notable share of tooth surface and cause sensitivity, and that about half of veneers need re-treatment or replacement after ten years, though it flags that this figure needs verification [1]. Press-on covers are marketed as avoiding tooth preparation; no studies of their fit, safety or longevity were found.

timeline.event: Charles Pincus invents veneers for film actors [1].
